Examining the reproductive biology of Odorrana swinhoana reveals distinct size thresholds that govern life history transitions. Field surveys indicate that metamorphosis is achieved at a snout-vent length of approximately 2.3 cm , a size that marks the completion of the dramatic morphological transformation from a gill-breathing tadpole to a terrestrial juvenile form. Following metamorphosis, individuals enter a prolonged growing phase. Females initiate reproductive maturation upon reaching a body size of 7.06 cm [Lp = 7.06 cm], whereas males begin the pubertal transition at a considerably smaller snout-vent length of 5.06 cm [Lp = 5.06 cm]. This divergence in size at sexual maturation between the sexes is a common pattern among ranid frogs, often attributed to the differential energetic demands of gamete production. The ultimate snout-vent length attainable by adult females in this species is 9 cm [Li = 9 cm], a size that represents the upper boundary of somatic growth. By contrast, adult males reach a smaller maximum snout-vent length of 7.5 cm [Li = 7.5 cm], a difference that likely reflects sexual dimorphism in resource allocation toward reproductive versus somatic tissues.

The wet mass of newly hatched individuals provides a baseline for understanding the growth trajectory of this species. At the moment of eclosion from the gelatinous egg mass, a neonate typically weighs approximately 0.0141 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0141 grams], a value consistent with the relatively small egg diameter of roughly 3 mm. This initial mass is modest, reflecting the limited yolk reserves available to support the endotrophic tadpole during its early development. As the tadpoles progress through the aquatic larval stage and approach metamorphosis, they accumulate considerable biomass. By the time females reach the pubertal snout-vent length, their body mass has increased dramatically to about 40.6 g [Wwp = about 40.6 g]rams, reflecting the substantial somatic investment required to support the development of a large clutch of yolked oocytes. In contrast, males at the onset of sexual maturation attain a wet body mass of only 14.8 g [Wwp = 14.8 g]rams, a value that underscores the comparatively lower energetic cost of spermatogenesis relative to vitellogenesis.

Gonadal maturation in this species is strongly influenced by seasonal thermal regimes, particularly during the cooler months when reproductive physiology is activated. Quantitative assessments from field-collected specimens reveal that the gonadosomatic index (GSI) reaches a mean value of 15% [GSI = 15%] at a water temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. This elevated index indicates that ovarian development and testicular recrudescence are actively underway during the winter period, even though oviposition itself typically occurs later in the spring when temperatures have risen.

Developmental rates during the embryonic phase are highly dependent on ambient thermal conditions, as with most amphibians. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C], the interval from oviposition to the rupture of the chorion and emergence of the free-swimming larva spans approximately 45 days [ab = approximately 45 days]. This developmental period is a critical window during which the embryo is entirely reliant on its yolk supply, and the rate of embryonic differentiation is tightly coupled to temperature. At lower thermal regimes, such as the 10 °C [T = 10 °C] conditions that trigger gonadal recrudescence, the incubation period would likely be extended considerably. The hatching success and quality of the yolk-sac larva are thus intimately tied to the thermal history of the breeding site, which in the montane streams typical of this species can vary markedly across the breeding season. Field observations confirm that females typically select oviposition sites that buffer against extreme thermal fluctuations.

Longevity data for Odorrana swinhoana compiled from mark-recapture studies in Taiwan's riparian habitats offer insights into the species' life history pace. The maximum lifespan recorded for individuals in the wild reaches approximately 11 years [am = approximately 11 years], a duration measured under the prevailing environmental conditions, which average about 17 °C [T = 17 °C] in the stream habitats where this species is most abundant. This relatively extended lifespan for a frog of its body size suggests a life history strategy that prioritizes iteroparity, allowing females multiple reproductive seasons to compensate for potentially variable recruitment success. The age at birth was documented at 45 days [ab = 45 days] under the same thermal regime of 17 °C [T = 17 °C], providing a clear benchmark for the duration of the embryonic period. The long adult lifespan, combined with a moderate age at first reproduction, positions this species as a slower-paced strategist within the ranid lineage, likely an adaptation to the stable but resource-limited montane stream ecosystems it inhabits.
